extracted.intended_audience: MER organizers, mathematics education researchers, conference/workshop planners, and mathematicians interested in math-education reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing MER special sessions, workshops, banquets, and advisory activities — covering attendance, pedagogy, format, outcomes, outreach, and logistics. Intended to guide evaluation of MER events and similar mathematics-education forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance as a popularity indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Attendance levels (near-full room, standing-room-only) indicate the popularity of talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MER sessions were often nearly full and a few were so crowded that there was standing room only for late-comers — used as evidence that talks were popular. Poor attendance may indicate topic/time mismatch. Organizers should anticipate audience size when arranging rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Room arrangements and capacity planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Room size and seating arrangements should match anticipated audience; AMS makes room arrangements in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMS assigned mid-sized hotel halls (~200 seats) for MER sessions; despite large overall meeting size (~4000 people), mismatches occurred (some sessions too crowded, some drew small crowds). Proper advance anticipation of audience size and room allocation affects accessibility and perceived success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program listing and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion in the conference program and scheduling across meeting days contributes to visibility and reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MER's special sessions were listed in the conference program and spanned the majority of the first two of the three-and-one-half day meeting — a factor enabling attendance. Timing of sessions (time of day) can affect turnout (some topics at poor times drew fewer attendees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic relevance and alignment with MER mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Session topics should center on mathematics education reform and relevant subtopics (K-12, undergraduate, portfolios, teacher prep, curriculum reform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of successful topics: 'Portfolios and interactive questionnaires', 'Introductory college mathematics: The critical filter for the majority', 'Trigonometry on the Ferris wheel: A constructivist approach.' Sessions aligned with MER's mission and addressing controversial or underserved areas (e.g., K-12) were seen as important contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical quality of presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenters should model good pedagogy — balance presentation with interactive elements and opportunities for reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good pedagogy was explicitly praised when presenters engaged audiences in lengthy discussions. Conversely, many sessions were described as lecture-oriented ('presenters “presented” [and] did not model good pedagogy'), and participants desired more modeling of reform-oriented classroom techniques, especially in breakout sessions. Recommendation: short presentation followed by structured discussion to model pedagogy while being time-efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of lecture vs interactive formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should balance efficient information transfer (lectures/panels) with interactive, hands-on activities and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morning panels (90 min) were effective at sharing information in a condensed timeframe but often didactic; afternoon breakout sessions (limited to ~15 participants) were intended to be more interactive. Some participants valued lecture-efficiency given time constraints; others wanted more interactivity. Organizers must weigh time efficiency against pedagogical modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of sessions (learning, networking, support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usefulness measured by whether participants learned new information, made personal contacts, and found emotional/professional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey respondents most commonly cited (1) learning new/eye-opening information, (2) networking (meeting and maintaining contacts), and (3) emotional support for educational endeavors. Majority who attended special sessions reported them useful. Usefulness should be measured along these dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence on attendance decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which special sessions/workshops influence participants' decisions to attend the larger meeting or MER workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey categories recorded: Not at all / A little / Considerably / Very much. Most respondents indicated special sessions did not influence their decision to attend the Joint Meeting; few said sessions strongly influenced attending MER workshops. This metric helps evaluate pull-effect of programming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banquet format effectiveness for networking
rubrics_metrics.description: Banquet design (cocktail hour, small-group seating, no after-dinner speakers) should facilitate informal networking among like-minded attendees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MER banquet had cocktail hour then round tables seating eight with no after-dinner speakers, enabling extended small-group discussion. Ticket sales and high recommendation rates (e.g., 73% of mathematicians who attended would recommend it) used as evidence the format met audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affordability and access for trainees
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost of events (banquet fee, travel/conference fees) affects graduate student and other participant attendance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A $45 banquet fee was probably too expensive for graduate students; respondents' willingness to attend another workshop dropped significantly if they had to pay own transportation/conference fee or all expenses. Use 'all expenses paid' vs 'self-pay' questions to gauge sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of communication/outreach channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Different communication methods (word of mouth, newsletters, listserver) have distinct roles in spreading information and maintaining contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word of mouth appeared most effective at initiating interest, while newsletters were better at maintaining communications. Recommendation: expand listserver(s), allow forwarding to facilitate electronic word-of-mouth. Evaluate channels by reach and initiation vs maintenance effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to present a range of views and spark discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing a forum for diverse and even controversial views is a value, measured by the extent of audience engagement and lively discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversial talks (e.g., 'What about the top 20%?') spurred lively debate; MER intentionally invited provocative presenters to stimulate dialogue. Success can be measured by audience reaction and post-session discussion quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant composition and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should attract a mix of university mathematicians, K-12 educators, education department representatives, and agency staff as appropriate to workshop goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baton Rouge workshop had ~60.5% university math department, 22.3% K-12 educators, with others from education divisions and agencies. Diverse participation supports cross-level exchange and is a metric of outreach success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop structure and scheduling (panels + breakout design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard MER workshop pattern: reception/keynote, morning panels, concurrent afternoon breakouts, and reflective Sunday panels to set future agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morning panels of 90 minutes with 2–4 speakers shared condensed information; afternoon 90-minute breakout sessions limited to ~15 participants facilitated interaction. Sunday reflections helped set next steps. Evaluate whether this structure meets goals of information transfer and participant interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation data collection and response rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect participant feedback via questionnaires; response rate affects interpretation validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Baton Rouge, 27 of 57 participants returned surveys (47.4% response). Use appendix survey instruments; interpret results considering response bias and representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome: validation and planned incorporation into practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should help participants validate existing practices and/or plan to incorporate new ideas into classes, department policies, or teacher-prep activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many participants reported the workshop validated their ideas or provided new items they planned to implement or share with colleagues or administrators. Success measured by self-reported intent to change practice and subsequent dissemination actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Face-to-face informal interaction value
rubrics_metrics.description: In-person, informal interactions (meals, receptions, dinner conversations) are particularly valuable for learning and networking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants reported learning most in informal settings and valuing the chance to ask questions and make reports 'come alive.' Event design should preserve time/space for informal exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff between pedagogical modeling and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizers must balance modeling interactive pedagogy (which may take more time) against the efficiency of lecture formats for sharing information in limited time frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some participants argued that interactive small-groups are not efficient for short workshops, while others wanted more modeling of classroom techniques. A hybrid approach (short presentation + structured discussion) was suggested as a compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness relative to peer organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: MER should be distinct in addressing controversial educational issues and K–12 topics where other societies (e.g., MAA, AMS) may focus elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-directors view MER as addressing more controversial topics and K-12 issues than MAA (which focuses on post-secondary). A metric of success is whether MER increases total educational sessions offered and covers unique content areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory Committee membership criteria and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisory Committee members chosen for experience in education activities and leadership; committee advises co-directors but does not set policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership selection: experience in education activities, leadership positions in mathematics and K-12 communities, and professional societies. The committee meets annually (limited face-to-face time) and provides long-range planning input, funding examination, and dissemination strategy advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of meeting audience needs (ticket sales and recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained ticket sales and high recommendation rates indicate that event formats meet audience needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-directors cite continued ticket sales and high recommendation percentages (e.g., 73% of mathematicians who attended banquet would recommend it) as evidence the banquet format meets needs. Track repeat attendance and recommendation rates as indicators.
